name: Reed's Law
statement: The value of a group-forming network can grow exponentially with its members.
meaning: In a network where members can freely form arbitrary subgroups — not just one-to-one links — the dominant source of value is the sheer number of distinct groups that can form. Because possible subgroups multiply exponentially with membership, Reed argues that beyond a certain scale group-forming value overtakes both broadcast and pairwise-connection value.
mechanism: A set of n members has 2^n possible subsets. Excluding the empty set and the n single-member sets leaves 2^n − n − 1 possible groups of two or more. That exponential term grows far faster than the pairwise-connection count of Metcalfe's law, about n². Reed calls networks that draw their worth from this the group-forming networks.

examples.text: Social platforms with communities — group chats, servers, subreddits, workspaces — derive much of their value from users self-organising into many overlapping groups, the phenomenon Reed's 2^n term is meant to capture. Illustrative of the model's intent rather than proof it scales that way.

A one-to-one messaging network is Metcalfe territory: value tracks the number of possible two-party links, about n², with no combinatorial group explosion. Reed's claim is that group-forming networks eventually leave that curve far behind.

variants.name: Sarnoff's law
variants.text: The linear floor of the trio: the value of a one-to-many broadcast network is proportional to its audience, n. Each additional viewer adds a constant increment.

variants.name: Metcalfe's law
variants.text: The quadratic middle: the value of a two-way network grows with the number of possible pairwise connections, about n². The escalating hierarchy runs Sarnoff (linear) to Metcalfe (quadratic) to Reed (exponential).

whyItMatters: It offered the most optimistic account of network value in the internet era, formalising the intuition that platforms enabling communities are worth more than those enabling mere connections. It sits at the top of the Sarnoff–Metcalfe–Reed hierarchy and shaped how the value of social and group-forming platforms was argued.

working.lead: Value group formation, not just connection
working.text: where a network lets members form arbitrary subgroups, the combinatorial explosion of possible groups is where Reed locates the outsized value.

working.lead: Treat the exponential as a ceiling, not a forecast
working.text: the 2^n count of possible subgroups is exact arithmetic, but real value follows only the tiny fraction of groups that actually form — so do not price a network at 2^n.
cognitive bounds like Dunbar's number mean most theoretically possible subgroups never form, so real high-value structure is far sparser than the formula implies.

limits: The exponential claim is contested. Briscoe, Odlyzko and Tilly ('Metcalfe's Law is Wrong', IEEE Spectrum, 2006) argue both Metcalfe's n² and Reed's 2^n are substantial overstatements, and that network value more realistically grows like n·log(n); they note that adding ten people would, under Reed, multiply value a thousandfold, which soon implies absurd totals. Human cognitive limits mean most possible subgroups never form. The 2^n counting of subgroups is exact, but the claim that value actually scales that way is disputed and widely regarded as overstated. The competing n·log(n) figure is itself debated in later literature.
misreadings: It is a combinatorial model, not an empirically established law: counting subgroups is exact, but equating that count with realised value is the contested leap. It does not mean a real platform's worth doubles with each new member — the vast majority of possible groups never form, and rigorous critiques put real growth far below exponential.
origin: Proposed by the computer scientist David P. Reed around 1999–2001, notably in his essay 'That Sneaky Exponential' and the article 'The Law of the Pack' (Harvard Business Review, February 2001). Reed set out the Sarnoff–Metcalfe–Reed trio of linear, quadratic, and exponential network value.

sources.text: Reed's law, Wikipedia. — the 2^n − n − 1 formula, the group-forming-network concept, and the HBR 2001 origin.
Briscoe, B., Odlyzko, A. & Tilly, B. (2006). "Metcalfe's Law is Wrong." IEEE Spectrum. — the n·log(n) critique of Metcalfe's and Reed's laws.
